After the American Revolution, tens of thousands of Americans who had stayed loyal to the British crown left the new United States for the British colonies to the north. Most went in 1783 and 1784, when the war ended and they faced seizure of property and threats at home.

Somewhere around 40,000 to 50,000 people moved north. Most settled in Nova Scotia, where New Brunswick was split off for them in 1784, and along the upper St. Lawrence and Lake Ontario, which led Britain to create Upper Canada, the later Ontario, in 1791. Among them were:

  • farmers, merchants and officials of many backgrounds
  • Haudenosaunee allies of Britain led by Joseph Brant, who got land on the Grand River
  • Black Loyalists, many of them people who had escaped slavery, some of whom later moved to Sierra Leone

The Loyalists gave English speaking Canada its start and a lasting suspicion of the American republic. The title "United Empire Loyalist" was given to them by Lord Dorchester, governor of Quebec.
